title: 4 industry experts say what has changed in raising a Series A in Africa
summary: Raising a Series A in Africa looks very different from the boom years of 2021 and 2022. Four investors explain why profitability, governance, debt financing, and local capital now matter more than growth at all costs.
full_text: 4 industry experts say what has changed in raising a Series A in Africa Raising a Series A in Africa looks very different from the boom years of 2021 and 2022. Four investors explain why profitability, governance, debt financing, and local capital now matter more than growth at all costs. Fewer than 10% of African startups that raise seed funding go on to secure Series A funding. In 2022, startups raised Series A within 18 months of their seed funding, but those in 2022 did so after 29 months, according to a Condia report. 2022 was the peak funding year. Now, the questions investors ask before writing a cheque have changed. We spoke to four experts to get insights into what has changed in raising a Series A. A higher financial performance bar  The consistent theme among all investors was high profitability metrics. Before, it was a nice-to-have; now, it is an entry requirement.  Joe Kinvi, Founder of Borderless, said,  “In 2022, at the height of ZIRP, many companies raised funds without real Series A fundamentals. Cheap capital was everywhere, so more companies raised more money than their traction warranted. Then the capital dried up towards the end of that year. Investors sobered up. And at almost the same time, African currencies underwent rapid devaluation. That hit a specific kind of company hard: those that are raised in USD but earn revenue in local currency. A startup that needed to hit $500K a month to qualify for a Series A now had to earn nearly double that in local currency terms to meet the same metrics.” “The biggest shift was investor confidence and what investors were willing to fund. Between 2022 and 2025, there was a clear move away from flashy fintech ideas and aggressive growth narratives toward businesses that could demonstrate profitability, operational discipline, and sustainable scale,” said Ivan Kadiri, Associate Vice President – Business Development & Relationship Manager (Fintechs) Folakemi Osho, General Manager, HoaQ, buttressed the point: “The winners in 2024/2025 were founders who treated Series A as validation of systems already working, not capital to fix broken ones. At the same time, conviction shifted from growth storytelling to reference density: multiple independent signals that the business would scale predictably.” All this is evidenced by the fact that it’s the strong, foundational startups with proven unit economics that get this funding, and even so, it is usually a mix of debt and equity with a smaller ticket size. Read also: From founders to funders: 12 Y Combinator alums backing the next generation of startups Smaller ticket sizes The average Series A equity ticket size was $15m in 2022 and dropped to $8.7m in 2023. Several say global VC firms anchored it, and the ecosystem is maturing, hence the correction underway. It’s now gaining, as the 2025 average ticket size was $16.8m. “By 2023, that changed materially. Series A became one of the hardest rounds to raise in Africa — deal frequency slowed, fundraising cycles lengthened, and many founders stayed in seed longer or raised bridge rounds instead. By 2025, while Series A activity had begun to recover, investors were underwriting very different fundamentals: retention, margins, governance, and clear paths to profitability. What changed wasn’t just the amount of capital available, but the quality bar required to access it,” said Founding Partner, HoaQ Nubi Kay. For founders, this meant runway planning became conservative. Investors will likely favour staged tranches over large upfront rounds, as seen in Nala’s May 2026 raise. The conversion rate between seed and Series A The seed-to-Series A pipeline collapsed significantly. The 2021-2023 seed cohort is converting to Series A at a lower rate than the 2019 cohort. 81 out of the 2022 seed cohorts have yet to raise a Series A after 28 months and counting. Investors say seed capital was in surplus at the time and was given to startups that should have been funded, but now they haven’t matured enough to secure follow-on funding or a Series A round. “Over 100 startups raised a seed round in 2022, compared to just 42 in 2025. As fewer companies entered the funnel, the number that would naturally graduate to Series A declined accordingly.” Kinvi added  Kinvi also claimed the funders moved up. “Early-stage investors who used to write pre-seed and seed cheques started chasing pre-Series A deals and beyond. That pulled capital away from the earliest stage, further tightening the top of the pipeline.” The result is what industry leaders call the “missing middle”: a gap between seed-stage startups that did not make it to Series A and the few breakout startups that do. Debt became a major source of capital Condia invited industry experts to a space to explain why this is the case. At the growth stage, it is mostly debt. Three years ago, debt financing was an afterthought, used primarily by fintechs managing loan books. Venture debt across Africa reached $1.64 billion in 2025, accounting for 41% of all capital deployed.  Founders use debt to extend runway between equity rounds, avoid excessive dilution, and demonstrate capital discipline to Series A investors.  Investors caution, however, that debt is not a substitute for equity at the earliest stages, and that founders who take on debt without understanding the repayment obligations have added a new category of risk to already complex businesses. Rise of local capital For years, the African startup ecosystem was dependent on foreign capital. Africa has witnessed the rise of local investor participation. In Bloomberg’s 25 startups to watch, the majority were funded by African investors. In 2025, local investors like Madica invested in more than two equity raises. In 2026, however, it’s mostly development finance institutions (DFIs)

title: Here is the reason CapitalSage acquired Chimoney to build the Africa–Canada payments corridor
summary: CapitalSage has acquired Chimoney weeks after its shutdown announcement. The deal gives CapitalSage a regulated Canadian payments infrastructure foothold and accelerates its Africa–Canada corridor ambitions.
full_text: Here is the reason CapitalSage acquired Chimoney to build the Africa–Canada payments corridor CapitalSage has acquired Chimoney weeks after its shutdown announcement. The deal gives CapitalSage a regulated Canadian payments infrastructure foothold and accelerates its Africa–Canada corridor ambitions. CapitalSage Vantage  Limited, a subsidiary of the Group, has acquired Chi Technologies Inc., the parent company of Chimoney, the Canada-based cross-border payment infrastructure startup, four weeks after its shutdown announcement. “I’m looking forward to Chimoney continuing its mission to unlock economic opportunities for everyone under the CapitalSage umbrella and structure. I’m confident the team will scale up governance, liquidity, and go-to-market capabilities,”  Uchi Uchibeke, founder and CEO of Chimoney, said. The acquisition will herald Capitalsage’s entry into the Canadian market. Know more about CapitalSage and Chimoney.  CapitalSage Holdings is well known in the ecosystem for its financial products, including Kolomoni. It raised ₦2.2 billion ($4 million) in debt, which was among the largest debt raises by an African financial technology startup in 2021. Its other subsidiaries are producers of FMCG products under the John Vents Cocoa Products brand. Chimoney was founded in 2022 by Uchi Uchibeke. Chimoney enabled businesses to pay freelancers and vendors in 41 currencies across Africa, North America, and Latin America. All with a single API.  Its thesis was to build a payment infrastructure that makes cross-border money movement as seamless as sending a message. It supported bank transfers, mobile money, airtime, gift cards, and stablecoin rails for off-ramps.  In 2023, it joined the Techstars Toronto accelerator. Chimoney raised less than  $1 million in total funding. It acquired Scrim, a social payments app, in 2023. Read also: Cross-border payment startup, Chimoney, shuts down after raising only $1 million in four years The exit and what comes next  The acquisition’s monetary value remained undisclosed. However, Uchibeke promised in an X post that “Every person who put capital into Chimoney will get their money back. That was the one thing I would not compromise on,” reiterating that this will be done at the close of the deal. The Chimoney team will also be beneficiaries of the deal’s proceeds.  Upon completion and relaunch, Chimoney will continue its day-to-day operations with plans to activate a US payments corridor. The Chimoney team, including Faheed Alli-Balogun (Head of Product) and Hammed Babatunde (Head of Operations), will join CapitalSage.  Uchibeke will lead the transition for six months before handing over operations to the CapitalSage team. He plans to build APort, a company focused on pre-action authorization for AI agents, which has already produced the Open Agent Passport (OAP).  The transaction will close in phases to accommodate Bank of Canada re-registration requirements under the Retail Payment Activities Act.   What’s at play Think of Chimoney as the rails; Capital Sage wants to expand its reach on.  In January 2026, the company was named one of Canada’s ten fintech startups to watch in 2026, cited specifically for holding both a FINTRAC MSB registration and a Bank of Canada PSP licence, a combination rare enough to be a differentiator in its own right. That framing matters for reading this acquisition. Canada’s fintech story, as observers were noting at the start of the year, had moved past the challenger bank era and into infrastructure. Chimoney was being positioned squarely in that category. CapitalSage is acquiring that position. Uchibeke said he preserved the licences, and that’s why the deal happened. For a multinational group already operating licensed entities across the UK, UAE, Nigeria, Kenya, and The Gambia, a Canadian entity with that regulatory footprint will do the heavy lifting. It also has a talent powerhouse of Group CEO Abiola Bawuah, who spent over 25 years in banking across Africa, most recently as CEO of United Bank for Africa’s operations across 20 countries, and founder and Group Managing Director John Adedamola Alamu, who built CapitalSage from a microlending operation in 2014. The acquisition also arrives at a moment when Canada’s fintech infrastructure layer is, by most accounts, still underleveraged. Chimoney was the only company on that January watchlist operating explicitly at the intersection of cross-border payments, digital identity, and AI agent infrastructure. That specificity — regulated wallets, W3C identity, policy controls for autonomous agents is what CapitalSage inherits, alongside the corridor ambitions. This is yet another exit via the merger-and-acquisition route, as predicted by industry experts in 2026.

Keypoints: Ramaphosa says migrants should not be blamed for South Africa’s challenges President calls for practical solutions to unemployment and crime Remarks come amid rising anti-immigrant tensions before local elections SOUTH African President Cyril Ramaphosa has urged citizens not to scapegoat migrants for the country’s economic and social challenges, saying frustration over unemployment and crime should be addressed through practical policies rather than hostility towards vulnerable communities. Speaking during the National Youth Day Commemoration in Johannesburg on Tuesday, Ramaphosa acknowledged widespread public concern over joblessness, crime and pressure on public services but argued that these longstanding problems require domestic solutions. His comments came as anti-immigrant sentiment intensified in parts of the country ahead of municipal elections later this year, amid the growing anti-migrant movement ahead of South Africa’s local elections. President calls for ‘practical solutions’ Ramaphosa said young South Africans were justified in expressing concern over the country’s economic conditions, particularly given persistently high youth unemployment and ongoing inequality. However, he cautioned against directing blame at foreign nationals living in the country. ‘Addressing these challenges requires practical solutions, not the scapegoating of vulnerable people,’ the president said during the event. He added that while his administration recognised concerns surrounding illegal immigration and was taking action to address them, including the government’s tougher migration enforcement measures, South Africa’s broader difficulties were largely home-grown. ‘Even as we recognise the challenge of illegal immigration – which we are taking decisive action to address – our problems are in the main our own problems, and we have a responsibility to fix them ourselves,’ he said. Economic pressures fuel public frustration South Africa continues to grapple with severe economic and social pressures. Youth unemployment remains among the highest globally, while violent crime and deep inequality continue to weigh on communities more than three decades after the end of apartheid. Those conditions have contributed to growing resentment among some groups, who argue that undocumented migrants increase competition for jobs and strain public resources. Many economists and policy experts have argued that structural economic weaknesses, sluggish growth and governance challenges are among the key factors contributing to the country’s economic difficulties. Recent weeks have seen protests and, in some areas, attacks targeting foreign nationals from elsewhere in Africa, echoing Ramaphosa’s earlier condemnation of anti-migrant violence. Some of the unrest has also mirrored recent incidents that left several Mozambican citizens dead, underscoring the regional implications of recurring xenophobic attacks. Tensions rise before elections Ramaphosa’s remarks also come against the backdrop of campaigning ahead of municipal elections scheduled for November, with his governing African National Congress under pressure amid years of declining electoral support and public dissatisfaction over economic performance and service delivery. Some anti-immigrant groups have publicly called on undocumented foreigners to leave the country by a self-imposed June 30 deadline, raising concerns that tensions could escalate further. Regional migration remains significant As one of Africa’s largest economies, South Africa continues to attract migrants from neighbouring states seeking employment opportunities, as well as people fleeing insecurity and instability elsewhere on the continent, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Ramaphosa’s intervention seeks to strike a balance between enforcing immigration laws and discouraging rhetoric that blames migrants for broader socioeconomic problems. Keypoints: Exiled opposition figure provisionally loses nationality Human Rights Watch raises due process concerns Decision deepens post-coup political tensions NIGER’S military authorities have provisionally stripped exiled opposition figure Mariama Djibrine of her nationality, prompting renewed criticism from Human Rights Watch (HRW) and raising concerns about the use of state powers against political opponents. The case has renewed debate over whether counterterrorism powers are being used to curb political opposition and restrict civil liberties in post-coup Niger, with rights groups warning that security measures should not undermine due process or democratic participation. HRW raises alarm over June 11 decree According to Human Rights Watch, a June 11 decree signed by General Abdourahamane Tiani provisionally removed Djibrine’s Nigerien nationality. The organisation said the action was linked to a 2024 order establishing a national database of individuals suspected of terrorism. Djibrine, who lives in exile, leads the Alliance des Démocrates du Sahel, a coalition of opposition figures from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso advocating a return to constitutional governance across the region. The authorities have accused her of spreading information likely to disturb public order, inciting revolt and collaborating with a foreign power. HRW contends that the case reflects a broader pattern of restrictions on dissent following the military takeover. Citizenship is widely recognised as a fundamental legal status, and rights advocates argue that provisionally withdrawing it from political opponents risks turning it into a tool of political pressure, particularly where due process protections are questioned. Political tensions remain high Djibrine has publicly called for the release of former President Mohamed Bazoum, who has remained in detention since being removed from office during the July 2023 coup. His continued detention has drawn international attention and remains one of the most contentious issues surrounding Niger’s transition under military rule. Human Rights Watch noted that Niger’s authorities previously used the same terrorism-related framework to provisionally remove the nationality of nine people associated with former President Bazoum, suggesting an expansion of the policy beyond former government officials. For opposition groups, the latest measure reinforces concerns that political activity conducted from abroad could still expose individuals to punitive action at home. Wider concerns over civic space The nationality decision comes amid broader restrictions on media, political activity and civil society in Niger. Since taking power, the junta has defended many of its actions as necessary to preserve national security while confronting persistent threats from armed extremist groups operating across the Sahel. Human rights organisations, however, have repeatedly warned that broad security powers should not come at the expense of freedom of expression, political participation and fair legal process. The debate reflects a wider challenge facing several countries in the region as governments seek to balance counterterrorism operations with respect for democratic norms and the rule of law. Security crisis complicates governance Niger continues to face attacks from armed groups linked to extremist organisations operating near its borders with Mali, Burkina Faso and Nigeria. The deteriorating security environment has strengthened the junta’s argument that extraordinary measures are needed to combat terrorism. At the same time, rights organisations have documented allegations of abuses committed by both armed groups and state security forces, highlighting the complex humanitarian and security challenges confronting the country. Against this backdrop, decisions affecting citizenship and political participation are likely to attract continued international scrutiny. Regional implications The case also reflects broader political trends across the Sahel, where military-led governments have increasingly emphasised sovereignty and security while facing criticism over restrictions on opposition movements and independent institutions. As regional alliances evolve and transitions to civilian rule remain uncertain, developments in Niger are likely to shape wider debates over governance, accountability and civil liberties across West Africa. For now, the provisional removal of Mariama Djibrine’s nationality has become another flashpoint in Niger’s contested political landscape, adding to concerns about the future of democratic participation under military rule.The post Niger strips exiled critic of nationality first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: AFC commits $600m towards Dangote’s broader $7bn fertiliser expansion Nigeria’s urea production capacity is set to rise from 3m to 9m metric tonnes annually A planned 3m metric tonne plant in Ethiopia is intended to bolster Africa’s fertiliser supply AFRICA Finance Corporation (AFC) has committed $600m towards the Dangote Group’s wider $7bn fertiliser expansion programme, backing plans to significantly increase urea production in Nigeria and develop a new manufacturing facility in Ethiopia as Africa seeks to strengthen food security and reduce dependence on imported agricultural inputs. The financing marks one of the continent’s most ambitious industrial agriculture investments in recent years. By supporting expanded fertiliser production across West and East Africa, the initiative aims to improve access to crop nutrients, reinforce regional supply chains and help countries meet rising food demand through greater domestic manufacturing. AFC expands support for strategic industry In an announcement issued on June 15, AFC said it would provide the financing facility to Greenview Fertilizer Corp., the entity identified by AFC in connection with the financing, as part of the group’s broader expansion strategy. The overall programme is valued at approximately $7bn, with AFC’s $600m commitment representing one component of the financing package rather than the full cost of the expansion. The plans include increasing annual urea production capacity in Nigeria from 3m to 9m metric tonnes and constructing a new 3m metric tonne fertiliser plant in Ethiopia. The announcement comes as major investment deals continue to reshape Africa’s industrial landscape, with strategic sectors such as manufacturing, infrastructure and energy attracting increasing flows of capital. Dangote Industries President and Chief Executive Aliko Dangote described the investment as ‘another important milestone in our long-standing partnership with AFC’. He said the planned expansion in Nigeria and Ethiopia would strengthen food security, improve agricultural productivity and deepen Africa’s industrial base, adding that AFC’s continued backing reflected confidence in the group’s ambition to build globally competitive industrial platforms. Expansion aims to strengthen food security Africa imports substantial volumes of fertiliser despite possessing significant natural gas reserves and agricultural potential. Urea fertiliser is one of the world’s most widely used crop nutrients, helping replenish soil fertility and improve yields, making it a critical input for boosting agricultural productivity and food production. Industry experts argue that increasing local production could improve supply reliability, reduce exposure to international price shocks and support higher crop yields across the continent. They also point to the need to unlock Africa’s own pools of domestic capital to finance transformative industrial projects. The planned increase to 9m metric tonnes of annual production would make Dangote Fertilizer one of the world’s largest urea production complexes if completed as envisaged, significantly strengthening Nigeria’s role in regional and international fertiliser markets. Meanwhile, the proposed Ethiopian facility, with an expected capacity of 3m metric tonnes annually, would reinforce the project’s ambition to create a pan-African fertiliser manufacturing network spanning West and East Africa, strengthening supply chains across multiple regions. Expanded production could also increase fertiliser exports to other African markets under the African Continental Free Trade Area, potentially reducing the continent’s dependence on overseas suppliers while supporting regional economic integration. The initiative complements Dangote’s growing export-oriented operations, highlighting the group’s broader industrial ambitions. AFC highlights long-term development goals AFC President and Chief Executive Samaila Zubairu said Africa would need to narrow a significant gap in fertiliser use and agricultural productivity to feed a population projected to reach 2.5 billion by 2050. He said supporting the expansion of the fertiliser platform would help improve food security, generate productive employment and strengthen the continent’s long-term economic resilience. The corporation also noted that the transaction follows the successful recycling of capital from earlier investments, including financing associated with the Dangote Refinery, allowing resources to be redeployed into new strategic infrastructure and industrial projects. Wider implications for Africa The expansion comes as governments across Africa seek to improve agricultural productivity while reducing vulnerability to disruptions in global supply chains. Greater regional fertiliser production could play an important role in lowering import dependence and supporting long-term food security objectives. If delivered on schedule, the expansion could reshape Africa’s fertiliser supply chain, reduce reliance on imports and strengthen the continent’s long-term food security and industrial resilience while reinforcing regional value chains.The post AFC commits $600m to $7bn Dangote fertiliser expansion first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Mission 300 has connected more than 50 million people across 40 countries The initiative aims to provide electricity to 300 million Africans by 2030 Tanzania, Ethiopia and Nigeria are among countries reporting significant gains MISSION 300, a joint electrification initiative led by the World Bank Group and the African Development Bank Group, has connected more than 50 million people to electricity across 40 African countries, according to the two institutions, marking early progress towards its goal of connecting 300 million people by 2030 in a continent where hundreds of millions still lack reliable electricity access. Launched in 2024, Mission 300 aims to connect 300 million people to electricity by the end of the decade through a combination of national grid expansion, mini-grids and stand-alone energy systems. The initiative builds on broader efforts to expand energy access across the continent, including initiatives explored in Africa Briefing’s report on Africa’s drive towards universal electricity access by 2030. Supported by partners including The Rockefeller Foundation, the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet and Sustainable Energy for All, the programme invests across power generation, transmission and the final connections that bring electricity directly to homes, businesses and public institutions. It also backs decentralised and off-grid energy solutions to extend access to remote and underserved communities. Earlier reporting by Africa Briefing detailed the scale of financing behind the initiative in its coverage of the World Bank-backed $50bn Africa electrification plan. Faster pace of electrification According to the World Bank and the African Development Bank, Mission 300 is now delivering electricity access at nearly twice the pace recorded before the initiative was launched. The institutions attributed the acceleration to increased financing, stronger policy commitments and improved coordination between governments, development partners and private investors. Tanzania has emerged as one of the programme’s biggest beneficiaries, with about 7.5 million people gaining access to electricity under Mission 300. Ethiopia has connected approximately 4.6 million people, supported by reforms intended to make grid connections more affordable. Nigeria has also reported notable progress, with more than 4.5 million people connected through private sector-led initiatives backed by public financing and development partners, demonstrating how blended funding models can encourage commercial investment in underserved markets. Billions committed to expanding access The World Bank Group and the African Development Bank Group said they have committed nearly $15bn in financing for Mission 300-related projects and mobilised about $4.5bn in co-financing. Other development partners have pledged more than $7bn to support Africa’s energy sector. The latest commitments add to previous funding announcements covered by Africa Briefing, including $6.15bn pledged for Africa’s Mission 300 power project, underscoring the growing financial backing behind efforts to accelerate electrification. The programme uses a mix of grants, guarantees and concessional loans to reduce investment risks and encourage private companies to expand services into communities that have historically been difficult or costly to reach. To date, 30 countries have launched National Energy Compacts — government-led roadmaps that set out reforms and investment priorities to strengthen electricity systems, expand renewable energy, improve regional integration and attract greater private sector participation. Burkina Faso, the Central African Republic, Djibouti, Gabon, Rwanda and Uganda are expected to unveil additional compacts during this week’s Africa Energy Forum. Leaders urge sustained momentum World Bank Group President Ajay Banga said the achievement reflected more than the number of connections made, adding: ‘Electricity is not just about power. It is about what it enables: jobs, business, health care, education and opportunity.’ African Development Bank Group President Sidi Ould Tah welcomed the progress but called on governments, investors and development partners to intensify efforts to achieve the programme’s 2030 target, highlighting the role of electricity in improving food security, healthcare outcomes and inclusive development. Supporting organisations also welcomed the milestone, arguing that coordinated financing and country-led reforms can help accelerate electrification across the continent. Closing Africa’s electricity gap Despite the reported gains, Africa continues to face the world’s largest electricity access challenge, with an estimated 600 million people still living without reliable power. Mission 300 was established to help close that gap by mobilising large-scale investment and encouraging reforms that make energy expansion more sustainable and commercially viable. Alongside the initiative, other flagship infrastructure ambitions such as Africa’s Grand Inga hydropower vision illustrate the scale of investment being pursued to transform the continent’s energy landscape. For many African countries, sustaining Mission 300’s current momentum will be critical to supporting industrialisation, expanding digital economies and improving living standards over the coming decade.The post Mission 300 reaches 50m electricity milestone first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Kenya is positioning itself as an AI hub UAE investment could accelerate digital transformation Smart cities and trade offer shared opportunities MORE than 15,000 delegates gathered in Nairobi for AI Everything Kenya and GITEX Kenya, underscoring the country’s growing role in shaping Africa’s artificial intelligence future. The event also reflects Africa’s broader push to invest in artificial intelligence, demonstrating that what Kenya and the continent are building in AI and digital innovation is no longer a distant aspiration but an emerging reality. Backed by sustained investment in digital infrastructure, forward-looking policy and an expanding technology ecosystem, Nairobi is reinforcing its position as one of Africa’s premier innovation centres. The gathering also sent a clear signal that the future of AI and the digital economy will increasingly be shaped by collaborative, inclusive and Africa-led innovation. The summit’s central message was unmistakable: Africa must move beyond conversations about AI and accelerate real-world implementation. For East Africa, that means embedding AI into healthcare, energy systems, public administration and financial services while cultivating researchers and entrepreneurs capable of developing technologies tailored to local needs. Kenya is laying the policy groundwork That transition is already underway. Last year, Kenya unveiled a five-year national artificial intelligence strategy requiring an estimated Sh152bn in investment to establish the country as Africa’s leading hub for AI research, innovation and deployment. Kenya’s proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill, currently before the Senate, similarly recognises that AI is becoming integral to governance, commerce, education, healthcare and democratic processes. If enacted in its current form, the legislation would establish an Office of the Artificial Intelligence Commissioner, an advisory committee, regulatory sandboxes, risk classifications and transparency requirements for public-sector AI deployment. Collectively, these measures aim to provide investors and technology partners with a predictable governance framework that prioritises ethics, accountability, data protection and human oversight. The UAE’s growing commitment to Africa Legislation alone cannot create a digital powerhouse. It also requires strategic partners with experience, investment capacity and a proven record of technological transformation. The United Arab Emirates has emerged as one such partner. Having established itself as one of the world’s leading digital economies, the UAE announced a $1bn AI for Development Initiative during last year’s G20 Summit to support digital infrastructure, government services and productivity improvements across Africa. As UAE Minister of State at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Saeed bin Mubarak Al Hajeri observed: ‘The UAE’s partnerships across Africa are well established, spanning more than 50 countries in areas such as sustainable energy, food security, infrastructure, education, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, and healthcare.’ His remarks underscore the breadth of the UAE’s engagement across the continent and its intention to deepen cooperation in sectors expected to drive future economic growth. Smart cities and digital trade converge The convergence of smart cities and digital trade represents one of the most promising frontiers for Kenya-UAE cooperation. Dubai Internet City offers an example of how long-term investment and targeted planning can foster a thriving technology ecosystem, providing lessons that may inform Kenya’s ambitions for Konza Technopolis. A smart city is not simply one equipped with sensors and digital dashboards. Rather, it is a city that uses data intelligently to improve everyday life. Artificial intelligence and advanced analytics can reduce congestion, minimise water losses, optimise waste collection, strengthen emergency response systems and simplify access to public services. Importantly, Kenya does not need to build entirely new cities to achieve these outcomes. Existing urban centres can integrate technology that improves both infrastructure management and service delivery. As Kenya seeks to cement its role as East Africa’s technology and trade gateway, Emirati investment in cloud computing and Arabic- and Swahili-optimised large language models could unlock significant opportunities in cross-border e-commerce and financial technology. The country’s digital credentials have also been strengthened by Kenya’s rapid uptake of AI technologies. AI-driven logistics, automated trade documentation and more sophisticated credit assessment tools could lower barriers for millions of small businesses operating across the region. In that scenario, digital infrastructure provides the platform while AI supplies the intelligence, positioning Nairobi not only as a smart city but also as a smart gateway to Africa’s digital economy. Balancing sovereignty and partnership Kenya and the UAE each contribute complementary strengths. Kenya offers an established innovation ecosystem, leadership in mobile payments and access to the wider East African market, while the UAE brings investment capital, global trade networks and extensive expertise in digital infrastructure. This complements the expanding UAE–Kenya economic partnership, which is opening new avenues for trade and technology collaboration. Michael Michie, co-founder and chief executive of EverseTech, argues that bilateral cooperation should ultimately benefit entrepreneurs on both sides. ‘The Kenya-UAE relations should help entrepreneurs in both markets access new customers. They should also make it easier for Kenyan technology companies to expand into the Gulf and for the UAE companies to use Kenya as a gateway into Africa,’ he says. Conversations during GITEX also highlighted the importance of balancing digital sovereignty with openness to international collaboration. Kenya increasingly approaches global partnerships not merely as a consumer of imported technology but as a country with growing infrastructure, skilled talent and a rapidly expanding digital market. For Africa, sovereignty should not mean technological isolation. Instead, it should involve carefully managed interdependence that preserves trust, protects data and enables innovation. Local cloud providers such as Servernah Cloud illustrate how domestic infrastructure can support sectors where control and security are paramount, including government, healthcare and financial services. Challenges remain While the opportunities are considerable, turning ambition into reality will require sustained investment, digital skills development, reliable energy infrastructure and affordable connectivity. Effective implementation of Kenya’s proposed AI governance framework will also be essential to building public trust, encouraging innovation and attracting long-term investment. Success will depend not only on technology itself but also on institutions capable of governing it responsibly and ensuring that innovation delivers broad-based economic and social benefits. Looking ahead The next chapter of UAE-Kenya relations may be defined less by physical infrastructure and more by what is built in the digital sphere. As Kenya advances its digital economy ambitions and the UAE strengthens its position as a global innovation leader, cooperation in AI, smart cities and digital trade offers a compelling platform for shared prosperity. Countries that successfully pair technological innovation with responsible governance are likely to shape the next phase of the global digital economy. Kenya and the UAE appear well positioned to pursue that opportunity together.  The post Why the UAE is betting big on Nairobi’s AI future first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Rising AI costs threaten Africa’s digital competitiveness Limited compute infrastructure risks deepening technological dependence Regional cooperation and local investment can narrow the affordability gap THE rising cost of artificial intelligence is quietly but decisively reshaping Africa’s technological trajectory. A troubling paradox is emerging across the continent: the technology widely celebrated as a catalyst for development is becoming increasingly inaccessible to many of the countries and institutions that could benefit from it most. This imbalance is more than a technical challenge. It represents a structural development issue with implications for economic competitiveness, digital sovereignty and Africa’s role in the global technology landscape. AI’s expensive foundation Unlike previous waves of digital transformation, artificial intelligence relies on a resource-intensive ecosystem. High-performance computing, cloud infrastructure, specialised semiconductors, large-scale data storage and highly skilled talent are all essential components of modern AI systems. Much of this infrastructure remains concentrated in a handful of global technology companies and markets, with pricing frequently denominated in US dollars. For many African economies, exchange-rate volatility and limited domestic capacity amplify these costs and reinforce dependence on foreign providers. Africa’s share of global high-performance computing infrastructure remains comparatively small, highlighting the continent’s limited ability to build and train advanced AI systems locally. Startups and universities face mounting barriers For startups, universities and public institutions, participation in the AI revolution is becoming increasingly expensive. Access to cloud computing resources, graphics processing units and application programming interfaces can consume budgets that would otherwise fund research or product development. These financial pressures are compounded by infrastructure challenges, including unreliable electricity supplies, uneven broadband access and high import costs for specialised equipment. The digital divide is therefore evolving. It is no longer defined solely by internet connectivity but increasingly by access to computational power and advanced machine intelligence. From digital divide to algorithmic dependence If these trends continue, Africa risks becoming dependent on AI technologies designed, trained and governed elsewhere. Systems developed using datasets that inadequately reflect African societies may struggle to address local realities or priorities. At the same time, reliance on foreign-owned infrastructure could expose governments and businesses to pricing changes, commercial decisions or geopolitical tensions beyond their control. Digital sovereignty increasingly depends not only on connectivity but also on the ability to create, adapt and govern intelligent systems domestically. Growing inequality within countries The affordability challenge could also widen inequality inside African economies. Large corporations and elite academic institutions may continue investing in AI capabilities, while smaller businesses, public agencies and rural innovators struggle to participate. Since small and medium-sized enterprises account for the overwhelming majority of businesses across Africa, restricted access to AI tools could constrain productivity gains and limit innovation. Education faces similar pressures. Many universities lack the computational resources needed to train sophisticated machine-learning models or conduct cutting-edge research, potentially widening the continent’s knowledge gap and reducing opportunities for home-grown innovation. Public sector ambitions meet fiscal reality Governments recognise AI’s potential across healthcare, agriculture, education, taxation and urban planning. Yet implementing these technologies requires substantial financial commitments at a time when many countries continue balancing competing development priorities. Pilot programmes have demonstrated promising applications, but scaling them nationally often remains difficult because of infrastructure and budget constraints. A strategic response is needed These challenges also create an opportunity for strategic thinking. Africa must adopt a multi-layered response that includes policy innovation, regional collaboration and indigenous solutions. As explored in ‘AI strategy matters more than AI tools’, sustainable technological progress depends not merely on acquiring AI applications but on building institutions, infrastructure and human capital that support long-term development. Governments and regional organisations should invest in shared computing infrastructure, encourage open-source AI development and strengthen research partnerships between universities and industry. Collaborative procurement could also reduce costs and improve bargaining power with global technology providers. Africa’s digital economy at stake Africa’s digital economy cannot reach its full potential if foundational AI technologies remain financially inaccessible. The broader growth opportunity is reflected in ‘Africa’s $469bn opportunity lies beyond taxes‘, which argues that innovation, digital infrastructure and skills development are central to unlocking sustainable prosperity. Investment in local talent should remain a priority. Building African expertise in AI research and entrepreneurship will reduce dependence on imported technologies while creating solutions tailored to local realities. Leadership and digital sovereignty Africa must approach AI not merely as another consumer technology but as a strategic asset. The continent’s demographic advantage can only be realised if affordability barriers are dismantled and local capabilities expanded. The importance of ownership and governance has also been emphasised in ‘Africa must own its AI future‘, which argues that African societies should shape the ethical and institutional foundations of emerging technologies rather than rely entirely on imported systems. Likewise, ‘AI, agency and Africa’s digital future’ highlights the need for the continent to retain strategic control over data, innovation and governance as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in economic and public life. A defining choice for Africa Artificial intelligence should be viewed not merely as another technology trend but as a strategic capability that will shape future economic growth and geopolitical influence. Africa’s youthful population and expanding innovation ecosystem provide significant advantages, but these strengths will only translate into lasting prosperity if access barriers are addressed. Without deliberate policy choices and sustained investment, the continent risks becoming a consumer rather than a creator of the next generation of intelligent technologies. The cost of AI is therefore more than a financial concern. It is a defining question about who will participate in shaping the digital future—and on what terms. Keypoints: Trust is economic infrastructure: Credible institutions and transparent financial systems can unlock investment, interoperability and long-term growth Reputation affects capital flows: Weak governance and trust deficits can deter foreign investment, increase risk and constrain cross-border finance Africa must build trust by design: Governments, regulators and businesses should prioritise digital identity, data standards and coordinated oversight to strengthen financial resilience THE development story of emerging markets over the past few decades has centred on infrastructure. Investments in payment rails, financial inclusion, mobile penetration, broadband access and digital services have addressed critical structural challenges and delivered meaningful progress. Yet infrastructure alone does not create interoperability, nor does it automatically guarantee participation in the global economy. As Africa is building the future of fintech, the continent’s next phase of growth will depend on trusted, interoperable systems that connect markets across borders. What ultimately enables countries to integrate successfully into international financial and digital systems is trust. By building credible institutions and making that credibility visible to the world, governments and businesses can unlock efficiencies that generate economic returns and broad societal benefits. There are already numerous examples of markets that have strengthened institutional credibility at scale, demonstrating that trust itself functions as economic infrastructure. For developing economies, the ability to engineer and sustain credibility carries measurable financial consequences. An IMF research paper on FATF grey-listing and capital flows, for example, found that capital inflows decline by an average of 7.6 percent of GDP after countries are grey-listed by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), alongside reductions in foreign direct investment and cross-border liabilities. Such findings highlight the urgent need for regulators and corporations to prioritise trust and credibility, not only to support inclusion and sustainable development but also to close interoperability gaps, a challenge reflected in Africa Briefing’s reporting on the FATF report warning of a global cyber fraud surge. Engineering trust as economic infrastructure Unlocking the next phase of financial maturity requires governments, regulators, investors, enterprises and consumers to rethink trust and perception as fundamental economic drivers. Perception matters because when economic actors believe risk is elevated, that perception influences capital allocation, pricing and market participation. Financial systems seeking long-term growth must therefore deliberately engineer trust as an asset rather than treat it as an intangible by-product. Pakistan offers a compelling illustration. The country’s previous episodes of FATF grey-listing reportedly contributed to an estimated cumulative GDP loss of around $38bn through weaker consumption, contracting exports and investor withdrawals before authorities undertook sustained reforms to restore confidence in financial transparency. Looking ahead, emerging economies are projected to record the world’s fastest fintech revenue growth by 2030, with Africa expected to expand by 13 times. Achieving that potential will require low-cost innovation, effective public-private collaboration and mobile-first delivery models that coordinate regulators with private enterprise. Such integration can strengthen financial interconnectedness while broadening access and making cross-border business easier. The growth of trusted payment ecosystems highlighted in Africa wallets power prepaid payments surge demonstrates how digital finance can accelerate inclusion and commerce across the continent. Building legible financial systems The next phase of digital growth depends on collective action. Responsibility cannot rest solely with governments or regulators; private-sector participants must also help make risk visible, understandable and manageable in real time. This evolving architecture relies on data intelligence, digital identity systems, transaction histories, behavioural signals, beneficial ownership records and effective reporting mechanisms. Initiatives such as Ghana’s rollout of payments on national ID cards illustrate how digital identity can strengthen trust and financial inclusion. From Singapore to Brazil, aspects of this model are already emerging. These developing markets are strengthening confidence through robust regulation, open finance frameworks and secure, standardised data-sharing across financial institutions. As ecosystems mature, interoperability becomes increasingly essential. Africa’s private sector is also beginning to expand its contribution, with companies like Cassava Technologies raising over $300M to strengthen digital infrastructure and cybersecurity across the continent, while Prembly’s FraudLens provides shared intelligence infrastructure. In practice, cyber resilience, regulatory coordination, fraud prevention and transparency can no longer be separated from broader economic policy. Governments must lead trust infrastructure Building digital trust cannot be left to startups or financial institutions alone. Governments must become architects of the underlying framework that supports confidence. Legal foundations should precede private innovation, while regulatory coherence should come before interoperability. Shared data standards, real-time reporting systems, beneficial ownership transparency and coordinated intelligence frameworks are no longer optional modernisation projects but central components of economic competitiveness. Regulators likewise have responsibilities that extend beyond enforcement. The strongest trust ecosystems are not those that conceal risks to protect reputations but those that demonstrate the institutional capacity to identify, disclose and address threats transparently. Governments therefore play a vital role in protecting the credibility of their markets through consistent regulation, transparent oversight and decisive responses to emerging risks. Investors should also reconsider how value is created in emerging economies, embedding trust-building into market development rather than viewing it merely as operational overhead or compliance expenditure. Financial institutions and enterprises, meanwhile, must strengthen governance, reporting standards and transparency as integral parts of long-term growth. Preparing for an AI-driven economy These priorities become even more pressing as artificial intelligence reshapes financial systems. Digital platforms are becoming increasingly interconnected, automated and potentially vulnerable to cascading failures. As the World Economic Forum has observed, digital resilience now depends on trust, information sharing and common standards as the digital attack surface expands exponentially. For Africa and other emerging markets, the next era of competitiveness will not be defined solely by physical or digital infrastructure. It will be determined by whether markets can demonstrate credibility, transparency and reliability at scale. Keypoints: Africa’s children are its most valuable long-term asset Investing in girls and education drives economic and social progress Governments must move from commitments to implementation on child rights AFRICA’S greatest resource does not lie beneath its soil. It walks to school each morning, fetches water from distant wells, studies by candlelight and dreams of a future better than the present. Every year on June 16, Africa commemorates the Day of the African Child. The occasion honours the thousands of schoolchildren who took to the streets of Soweto, South Africa, in 1976 to protest against the inferior education system imposed under apartheid. Many paid with their lives. Their sacrifice became an enduring symbol of the struggle for dignity, equality and the right to education. Fifteen years later, the Organisation of African Unity, now the African Union, established the Day of the African Child to ensure that the courage of the Soweto children would never be forgotten. More importantly, the day serves as a reminder that Africa’s future depends on how well it protects, educates and empowers its children. Africa’s demographic advantage This year’s commemoration comes at a pivotal moment for the continent. Africa is the world’s youngest region, with more than half its population under the age of 25. The United Nations projects that by 2050, more than one in four people globally will be African. The continent’s future prosperity, stability and global influence will be determined not by its mineral wealth or natural resources, but by whether its children are given the opportunity to realise their full potential. The 2026 Day of the African Child theme, ‘Ensuring Universal Access to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Every Child in Africa’, highlights a challenge affecting millions of children every day. Access to clean water and sanitation is not merely a development issue; it is fundamentally a children’s rights issue. Across Africa, millions of children still walk long distances to collect water. Girls bear a disproportionate share of this burden. Time spent fetching water is time lost from school, study and play. Inadequate sanitation facilities contribute to absenteeism among adolescent girls, particularly during menstruation. In conflict-affected areas, the search for water can expose women and girls to violence, harassment and exploitation. Yet water and sanitation represent only one chapter in a much broader story. Conflict and inequality steal childhoods Across the continent, millions of children continue to face threats that undermine their right to survive, learn and thrive. Armed conflicts in Sudan, the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Somalia and parts of the Sahel continue to disrupt childhoods on a devastating scale. Children are displaced from their homes, separated from their families and denied access to education, healthcare and protection. For girls, the consequences are often particularly severe. Conflict magnifies existing inequalities. Child marriage, sexual violence, trafficking and exploitation frequently increase during periods of instability. Families struggling with poverty and insecurity may view marriage as a coping or perceived safety mechanism. Armed groups may target girls for abduction or forced marriage. Schools are destroyed, occupied or abandoned, and girls are often the first to be withdrawn from education when resources become scarce. Even beyond conflict zones, harmful practices continue to rob millions of girls of their potential. Child marriage, female genital mutilation and discriminatory social norms remain persistent barriers to gender equality in several African countries. Investing in girls benefits everyone The numbers tell a sobering story. UNICEF estimates that more than 640 million girls and women alive today were married before their eighteenth birthday, while another 12 million girls are married each year. In Eastern and Southern Africa alone, more than 50 million women were married as children. UNICEF rightly describes child marriage as ‘a fundamental violation of human rights’. The consequences extend well beyond individual lives. The World Bank estimates that failing to educate girls costs countries between $15tn and $30tn in lost productivity and lifetime earnings. Girls who stay in school are more likely to delay marriage, enjoy better health outcomes, earn higher incomes and contribute more significantly to national development. Simply put, investing in girls is not charity. It is smart economics. The tragedy is that Africa continues to lose immense talent because of entirely preventable barriers. Every girl forced into marriage before adulthood could have become a doctor, engineer, entrepreneur, teacher, scientist or leader. Every child denied an education weakens Africa’s prospects for prosperity and peace. This should concern every African, whether leader or citizen. Turning commitments into action The African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child recognises every child’s right to education, health, protection and development. The challenge facing Africa today is not a lack of commitments. The continent has no shortage of declarations, policies or frameworks. The challenge is implementation. Governments must treat education as both a development priority and a national security imperative. Every child, regardless of gender, disability, location or economic status, deserves access to quality, inclusive education. Safe schools should be regarded as essential infrastructure for national development. Child protection systems must also be strengthened. Laws prohibiting child marriage, trafficking, exploitation and violence against children exist in many countries, but enforcement remains inconsistent. Governments should invest in implementation, accountability and survivor support services. Africa must significantly increase investment in girls. The evidence is overwhelming: educated girls marry later, have healthier families, earn more and contribute more to economic growth. If the continent is serious about achieving the ambitions of Agenda 2063, girls’ education must move from the margins of policy discussions to the centre. Harmful traditions that undermine children’s rights should be addressed through community-led approaches involving traditional and religious leaders, parents, educators and young people themselves. Culture evolves, and practices that harm children can and should change. Children must also be placed at the centre of peacebuilding and recovery efforts. Lasting peace cannot be achieved while generations grow up traumatised by conflict and violence. African governments, armed groups and international partners must intensify efforts to prevent the recruitment and use of children in armed conflict while ensuring the safe release, rehabilitation and reintegration of former child soldiers. Child protection, psychosocial support, education and meaningful youth participation should become integral components of peace processes and post-conflict recovery. Listening to the next generation Finally, Africa must listen to its children. The children of Soweto were not passive victims. They were courageous agents of change who demanded a better future. Across the continent today, young people continue to demonstrate leadership, resilience and innovation. They champion climate action, advocate for girls’ rights, develop technological solutions and transform their communities. They are not merely the leaders of tomorrow. They are already shaping Africa today. As we commemorate the Day of the African Child, we should remember a simple truth: Africa’s greatest resource is not gold, oil, diamonds or rare earth minerals. It is its children. The measure of Africa’s success in the coming decades will not be the size of its economies or the value of its exports. It will be whether every African child — girl or boy, rural or urban, living in peace or conflict — can realise their full potential. The children of Soweto marched for dignity, opportunity and justice. Half a century later, their message still echoes across the continent. The task before Africa is clear: protect, educate and empower every child. Keep the rights, safety and potential of African children where they belong — at the centre of Africa’s future. Because when African children thrive, Africa thrives. full_text: Cosmetics, food, beverages account for 50 per cent of counterfeits products —NAFDAC The National Agency for Food and Drugs Administration and Control (NAFDAC) on Wednesday said cosmetic products, food and beverages accounted for over 50 per cent of counterfeit products in the country. The National Agency for Food and Drugs Administration and Control (NAFDAC) on Wednesday said cosmetic products, food and beverages accounted for over 50 per cent of counterfeit products in the country. NAFDAC Director-General, Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, made this known at a news conference organised by the agency to commemorate the 2026 International Anti-Counterfeit Month observed globally in June. Adeyeye, represented by Dr Martins Iluyomade, the Director of Investigation and Enforcement, NAFDAC,  said the percentage was based on the volume of counterfeit and fake cosmetics, good and beverages confiscated by NAFDAC. She added that fake and substandard medicines containing incorrect ingredients, insufficient active pharmaceutical substances, or no active ingredients in circulation were also seized during its various operations across the country. “Cosmetics account for the most counterfeited products in Nigeria, followed by food and beverages, accounting for more than 50 per cent of seizures. “Pharmaceuticals also account for significant proportion of NAFDAC’s enforcement activities. The agency also raised concern over the evolving tactics used by counterfeiters to flood Nigeria’s markets with fake and substandard medicines, warning that the trend posed a serious threat to public health and national security. The D-G explained that the counterfeiters used online procurement systems that allowed individuals to order counterfeit products directly from foreign manufacturers without leaving Nigeria. She said they also exploited cargo consolidation systems, known as groupage, to smuggle products into the country. According to NAFDAC, under the groupage arrangement, multiple importers share a single shipping container, making it difficult for regulators to identify suspicious consignments. “Previously, importers had to travel abroad, inspect factories and arrange shipments themselves. “Today, someone can sit comfortably in a shop in Nigeria, place an order online, and have counterfeit products delivered to their doorstep through logistics companies. “These foreign companies have agents or suppliers that monitor products with high market demand and arrange for w counterfeit versions to be manufactured abroad, particularly in Asia. “These fake products often replicate the packaging of genuine brands so closely that consumers and even retailers struggle to distinguish them from authentic products,” he said. “No country in the world can effectively monitor every single package entering through such channels. “This has become a serious security concern, not just for medicines but for other regulated products,” she said. To address these challenges, NAFDAC said it had strengthened collaboration with security agencies, including the Nigeria Customs Service and other regulatory bodies. The D-G said the agency was also working to close regulatory loopholes and improve verification systems that allowed manufacturers to confirm whether imported shipments actually originated from their facilities. “This fight cannot be won by NAFDAC alone. “Government institutions, manufacturers, importers, logistics companies, healthcare professionals, media and consumers all have a role to play in safeguarding public health.” She also commended the judiciary for expediting the prosecution of drug-related cases and securing swift convictions for those involved in the manufactureing and distribution of counterfeit and illicit medicines. “We have had a number of convictions since last year. “The most recent was an individual that was sentenced to 40 years in prison in a case that started last November and completed in February,” she said. The agency urged Nigerians to remain vigilant, purchase medicines only from authorised outlets, verify products using available authentication technologies, and promptly report suspected counterfeit products to the appropriate authorities. The rollout, in Abuja on Wednesday, marks a major shift in Nigeria’s broadcast system after years of delays, with officials saying it would expand access to quality television, create jobs and improve information delivery nationwide. Speaking at the event, Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Dr Bosun Tijani, said the project is a key step in Nigeria’s wider digital transformation and economic plan. He also said the combination of fibre and satellite projects would strengthen Nigeria’s digital reach beyond its borders.“What you are seeing today is just a glimpse of what is to come,” he added. Also speaking, the Director-General of the National Broadcasting Commission, Mr Charles Ebuebu, said the project represents a new national communications system. Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mr Mohammed Idris, said the programme is the result of years of planning and coordination across agencies. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has dismissed fears that artificial intelligence will make humans obsolete, arguing instead that the technology will increase demand for workers and create new opportunities. Speaking at the VivaTech conference in Paris, Jeff Bezos pushed back against warnings from experts and policymakers who believe AI could lead to widespread job losses. He maintained that the technology would help remove barriers to growth and ultimately boost the need for human labour. “I know there’s a lot of concern that many people have, including many smart people, that AI is going to make humans redundant and so on,” Bezos said. “I totally disagree with this point of view. And I think, in fact, AI is going to create a labour shortage.” Bezos presented an optimistic vision of AI’s role in society, saying people are often constrained not by a lack of ideas but by limitations that technology can help overcome. The billionaire entrepreneur was discussing his latest AI venture, Prometheus, which aims to accelerate physical manufacturing, an industry that is becoming increasingly automated. His remarks contrast with concerns expressed by several political and technology leaders. Former British prime minister Rishi Sunak, who now advises Microsoft and AI company Anthropic, recently said artificial intelligence was already affecting employment prospects for young people. In Britain, the Trades Union Congress has warned that AI could repeat “the disaster of deindustrialisation”, with jobs being “degraded or displaced” while shareholders reap the benefits. However, the union also acknowledged that the technology has the potential to transform industries if deployed responsibly and that workers could share in productivity gains. Beyond artificial intelligence, Bezos used his appearance at Europe’s biggest technology exhibition to discuss the future of space exploration. He argued that the challenge facing humanity’s expansion into space was not a lack of demand but limited access, describing the sector as “supply constrained, not demand constrained”. According to Bezos, the Moon represents the ideal starting point for establishing a lasting human presence beyond Earth because of its proximity and available resources. “We’re going to the Moon to stay, not just to visit,” Bezos told the audience, adding that technologies such as electrolysis could one day allow lunar resources to be used to refuel spacecraft and support a permanent settlement outside Earth. The conversation also touched on Blue Origin, Bezos’s private space company, which is developing technologies aimed at expanding human activity beyond the planet. The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ogun State on Wednesday formally received former Senator, Iyabo Obasanjo, into its fold and immediately presented her with the party's flag as its senatorial candidate for Ogun Central, ahead of the forthcoming elections.

full_text: PDP receives Iyabo Obasanjo, unveils her as Ogun Central Senatorial candidate The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ogun State on Wednesday formally received former Senator, Iyabo Obasanjo, into its fold and immediately presented her with the party's flag as its senatorial candidate for Ogun Central, ahead of the forthcoming elections. The post PDP receives Iyabo Obasanjo, unveils her as Ogun Central Senatorial candidate appeared first on Vanguard News. By James Ogunnaike The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ogun State on Wednesday formally received former Senator, Iyabo Obasanjo, into its fold and immediately presented her with the party’s flag as its senatorial candidate for Ogun Central, ahead of the forthcoming elections. The development is viewed as a major boost to the PDP’s growing influence and acceptance across Ogun State, particularly in Ogun Central Senatorial District. Political observers believe that Obasanjo’s return to partisan politics under the PDP banner could significantly strengthen the party’s electoral prospects, given her extensive political experience, grassroots appeal and longstanding connection with the people of the district. Presenting the party’s flag to her, the State Chairman of the PDP, Abayomi Tella described Obasanjo as a valuable addition to the party and expressed confidence that her emergence would further energize the party’s support base across the state. Speaking after her formal reception, Obasanjo explained the circumstances led to her decision to leave the All Progressives Congress (APC), insisting that her political decisions had always been guided by principles of fairness, respect and service to the people. She disclosed that when she returned to active politics, she initially joined the APC because of the respect and recognition accorded her by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. She said, “when I returned to active politics, I chose to join the APC because President Bola Ahmed Tinubu treated me with great respect and dignity. He regarded me like his own daughter, gave me my rightful place, and accorded me the recognition I deserved. It was never about money; it was about respect”. According to her, honour and prestige remain fundamental values in Yoruba culture. “In Yorubaland, prestige and honour are often valued more than money. When you give me prestige and recognition, you earn my loyalty and respect in return,” she stated. The former senator stressed that she was not pressured into returning to politics, noting that it was the people of Ogun State who persuaded her to come back and contribute to the state’s development. “Nobody persuaded or begged me to join the APC. It was my people who called me back into politics. They told me that Ogun State was no longer the same as the one I left and urged me to return and contribute once again to its development. “I answered that call because the people still remembered the good work I did as a Senator and as a Commissioner in Ogun State. Their support and confidence inspired my return,” she said. Obasanjo, however, expressed disappointment over the process that produced the APC’s consensus governorship candidate, alleging that the procedure violated the spirit of consultation required under the party’s constitution. She said: “when I joined the APC, I committed myself fully to the party. I made it clear from the beginning that if the party adopted a consensus arrangement, I would respect and accept the outcome. “As part of the consultation process, we toured Ogun West and Ogun East and were preparing to move to Ogun Central before a meeting was suddenly called by the party leadership. “According to the APC Constitution, for a consensus candidate to emerge, all aspirants are expected to engage in discussions and consultations before any decision is announced. However, when we arrived at the meeting, a consensus candidate had already been announced.” The former lawmaker alleged that aspirants from Ogun Central and Ogun East were excluded from critical consultations. “We were informed that two aspirants from Ogun West had been persuaded to step down in support of the consensus candidate. At that point, I realized that something was wrong. “Ogun West alone cannot determine who becomes Governor of Ogun State. If consultations and negotiations were only held with aspirants from Ogun West while aspirants from Ogun Central and Ogun East were excluded, then the process could not be described as a genuine consensus,” she said. Obasanjo further argued that Ogun Central was unfairly sidelined in the sharing of key political positions in the state. “It is important to note that both myself and the PDP deputy governorship candidate are from Ogun Central. Yet, when the major political positions were shared among the four divisions of the state, Ogun Central was completely left out. “That raises serious questions about fairness, equity and inclusiveness in the political process,” she added. Speaking on her political journey and family background, Obasanjo highlighted the legacy of service associated with both her family and that of PDP governorship candidate, Hon. Ladi Adebutu. “Both Hon. Ladi Adebutu and I come from respected families with a long history of service to the people. Our fathers dedicated their lives to empowering others, creating opportunities and supporting countless individuals across Ogun State. “The number of people whose lives have been positively impacted by their generosity and commitment to humanity is immeasurable,” she said. She expressed confidence that the PDP would secure victory at the polls, insisting that the will of the people would ultimately prevail. “I remain convinced that the mandate of the people cannot be permanently denied. I believe that, by the grace of God and with the support of the good people of Ogun State, I will reclaim my mandate and continue the service I have always been passionate about. “What gives me confidence is the extraordinary love and acceptance I continue to receive from the people. I stayed away from active politics for over twenty years, yet the people never forgot me. They continued to remember my service, call my name and encourage me to return.” The post PDP receives Iyabo Obasanjo, unveils her as Ogun Central Senatorial candidate appeared first on Vanguard News.

title: Ronaldo kept quiet as DR Congo hold Portugal to 1-1 draw
summary:
Portugal were held to a 1-1 draw by the Democratic Republic of Congo on Wednesday as Cristiano Ronaldo played in a record-equalling sixth World Cup.

The post Ronaldo kept quiet as DR Congo hold Portugal to 1-1 draw appeared first on Vanguard News.
full_text: Ronaldo kept quiet as DR Congo hold Portugal to 1-1 draw Portugal were held to a 1-1 draw by the Democratic Republic of Congo on Wednesday as Cristiano Ronaldo played in a record-equalling sixth World Cup. The post Ronaldo kept quiet as DR Congo hold Portugal to 1-1 draw appeared first on Vanguard News. Cristiano Ronaldo’s record-equalling sixth World Cup got off to a disappointing start as the Democratic Republic of Congo secured their first ever point at the finals, drawing 1-1 with Portugal in their Group K match on Wednesday. Yoane Wissa’s header cancelled out Joao Neves’s early goal and the African side — appearing in their first World Cup since 1974 when it was known as Zaire — more than held their own. Ronaldo, 41, was largely a peripheral figure throughout the match — failing to make the impact his great rival Lionel Messi had done on Tuesday in scoring a hat-trick against Algeria. The DRC’s achievement was even greater given their preparations had been disrupted by the Ebola outbreak back in their country. Some Portugal players were wearing wrist bands, given to them by their Prime Minister Luis Montenegro, in tribute to late team-mate Diogo Jota, who was killed in a car crash last year. Portugal got off to the perfect start, with Neves powering home a header from Pedro Neto’s cross in the sixth minute. However, despite dominating possession they lacked a cutting edge and well into time added on in the first half their opponents made them pay. Wissa rose unmarked to head past Diogo Costa in the Portuguese goal sparking wild celebrations on the pitch, the bench and among the Congolese fans in the stadium as the Newcastle forward registered his country’s first ever goal at a World Cup. Former Portuguese defensive bulwark Pepe, watching from the VIP seats, did not look impressed. Bernardo Silva had started the day by joining Real Madrid on a free transfer but he ended it by watching from the bench after Martinez took him off at half-time. He was briefly off his feet celebrating when Joao Cancelo’s overhead kick hit the back of the net — only for it to be ruled out for offside. The Congolese were matching the Portuguese, though, and 35-year-old veteran striker Cedric Bakambu shrugged aside Bruno Fernandes, but his shot came back off the near post. Ronaldo finally had a chance to shine when presented with a chance by Francisco Conceicao’s pass but he fluffed his lines sending it wide of the post. The same combination linked up again minutes later, Conceicao — a far livelier presence than Silva had been — teeing up Ronaldo but once again the result was the same, the ball went wide. Portugal thought they had at least got a corner but when it was not given Conceicao slammed the ball into the ground in frustration as his side failed to pick up three points in their opener.
