Keypoints: Fitch says SSA economies are stronger than in 2022 Oil importers remain vulnerable to energy price shocks Fiscal reforms and reserves improve resilience SUB-SAHARAN African economies are entering the economic fallout from the recent Middle East crisis from a stronger position than they occupied during the commodity shock that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to Fitch Ratings. The agency says improvements in fiscal management, monetary policy and external balances have enhanced resilience across much of the region, although higher energy costs and inflationary pressures remain significant risks. In a report published on June 15, Fitch argued that the recent Middle East crisis will serve as an important test of economic reforms implemented across much of Sub-Saharan Africa since 2022. Many of these reforms have focused on strengthening public finances and improving tax collection, echoing broader debates around Africa’s revenue mobilisation challenge. While stronger foreign exchange reserves, lower current-account deficits and improved fiscal management have enhanced resilience, higher fuel prices, supply-chain disruptions and renewed inflationary pressures could still expose vulnerabilities in some of the region’s most import-dependent economies. The agency cautioned that the crisis has reintroduced risks linked to energy markets, inflation and government spending, particularly for countries heavily reliant on imported fuel. Oil importers remain most exposed Despite the easing of geopolitical tensions, global energy markets remain sensitive to developments in the Middle East, a region that remains central to global oil production and maritime shipping routes. Fitch identified higher energy import costs as the most immediate risk facing many African economies. Several countries across the region depend heavily on imported refined petroleum products, leaving them vulnerable to price swings and potential supply disruptions. Countries such as Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Senegal remain particularly exposed to higher fuel import costs, while oil-producing economies including Nigeria and Angola could benefit from stronger export earnings if elevated energy prices persist. The agency also warned of potential shortages of refined fuel products and fertiliser, both of which play critical roles in economic activity and food production. Such shortages could place additional pressure on consumer prices and complicate economic management. Governments may face difficult choices if fuel prices continue rising. While shielding consumers through subsidies or price controls can ease social tensions, such measures often come at a fiscal cost and can distort market incentives. Fitch noted that efforts to prevent the full pass-through of global fuel price increases may encourage speculative hoarding and artificially boost demand, exacerbating supply challenges. Growth outlook remains resilient Despite the risks, Fitch’s overall outlook for the region remains positive. The ratings agency expects all Fitch-rated Sub-Saharan African sovereigns to record economic growth in 2026. Median real GDP growth is projected at 4 percent, unchanged from 2025. That would leave Sub-Saharan Africa among the world’s fastest-growing regions despite heightened geopolitical uncertainty and persistent global trade tensions. The projection is broadly consistent with IMF forecasts showing Africa among the world’s fastest-growing regions, even as policymakers navigate an increasingly uncertain global environment. That forecast reflects stronger policy frameworks and improving economic fundamentals in several countries. Public-sector reforms, investment programmes and more stable macroeconomic conditions have contributed to a stronger growth foundation than existed during the 2022 commodity shock. Some countries may also benefit from higher prices for export commodities. For exporters of oil, minerals and other raw materials, stronger export earnings could offset part of the increase in energy import costs. However, the degree of protection varies significantly across the region. Net commodity importers remain considerably more exposed than exporters. Inflation risks re-emerge Higher fuel prices could reignite inflationary pressures across many economies. The risks mirror earlier warnings that rising crude prices could complicate monetary policy across Africa, particularly for net energy importers already managing elevated living costs. Energy costs influence transportation, agriculture, manufacturing and logistics, meaning sustained increases can spread quickly through broader consumer prices. Fitch said inflation is beginning to rise in some countries but noted that the increase is occurring from a relatively low base compared with the inflation surge that followed the Ukraine conflict. A key factor supporting resilience has been greater currency stability. Many African central banks tightened monetary policy aggressively over the past several years, helping to stabilise exchange rates and anchor inflation expectations. As a result, most central banks are currently operating with positive real policy rates, giving them greater flexibility to respond if inflation accelerates further. This marks a notable contrast with conditions in 2022, when policymakers across much of the region faced surging inflation and weaker monetary credibility. Stronger external buffers Fitch also highlighted significant improvements in external balances. Several sovereigns have narrowed current-account deficits, while foreign exchange reserves have strengthened. Most Fitch-rated countries now hold reserves equivalent to at least three months of current external payments. Greater exchange-rate flexibility has further enhanced resilience by allowing economies to absorb shocks more effectively. Fitch’s assessment comes as many African governments are attempting to consolidate fiscal gains achieved through recent IMF-backed reform programmes across the continent, subsidy rationalisation and stronger revenue collection. While these measures have improved resilience since 2022, a renewed surge in energy prices could complicate efforts to reduce debt burdens, contain inflation and rebuild fiscal buffers. For investors and credit markets, these improvements provide reassurance that many African sovereigns are better equipped to navigate periods of global uncertainty. Fiscal reforms face a fresh test Perhaps the most important question is whether recent fiscal gains can be maintained. Since 2022, governments across the region have intensified revenue mobilisation efforts and reduced costly subsidy programmes. These reforms have strengthened public finances and supported debt sustainability. Yet political and social pressures remain a challenge. Rising fuel costs often trigger public dissatisfaction, particularly where households are already struggling with living costs. Governments may therefore face renewed pressure to intervene. Fitch noted that fiscal support measures introduced so far have generally been limited in scale and duration. However, a prolonged period of elevated energy prices could increase demands for broader government assistance. For policymakers, the aftermath of the recent Middle East crisis represents more than a temporary external shock. The coming months will reveal whether the policy adjustments implemented since 2022 have fundamentally strengthened Africa’s economic resilience or merely improved its ability to withstand the next external shock.The post Fitch: Africa better prepared for oil shock first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Ghana is considering establishing a dedicated Auditors’ Court Reported financial irregularities rose to GH¢18.4bn (approximately $1.66bn) in 2024 The proposal forms part of wider efforts to strengthen fiscal accountability GHANA is considering creating a dedicated Auditors’ Court after reported financial irregularities across state institutions rose to GH¢18.4bn (approximately $1.66bn) in 2024, as the government seeks to strengthen public financial accountability. The proposal was announced by Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson during the inauguration of a new governing board for the Internal Audit Agency (IAA), which has also been tasked with supporting institutional reforms and reviewing the country’s Internal Audit Agency Act of 2003. The proposal forms part of broader efforts to strengthen public financial management and address weaknesses identified in recent audits while improving confidence in the stewardship of public resources, following IMF approval of Ghana’s latest reform review, which highlighted progress on fiscal and governance reforms. Proposal aims to strengthen accountability Forson said the government is considering a specialised Auditors’ Court to strengthen oversight and accountability within the auditing profession as part of wider governance reforms. Established under the Internal Audit Agency Act of 2003, the IAA coordinates and supervises internal audit activities across government institutions, develops audit standards, monitors compliance and supports the detection of control weaknesses and potential fraud risks. While the legislation outlines responsibilities for overseeing public-sector financial management, it does not create a dedicated judicial mechanism for adjudicating alleged misconduct involving internal auditors. The proposed court could create a specialised forum for addressing audit-related matters and complement existing oversight and disciplinary mechanisms by strengthening enforcement and professional accountability. No legislation establishing such a court has yet been introduced. Reported irregularities more than doubled The proposal follows the Auditor-General’s latest report on public boards, corporations and statutory institutions, which found that reported financial irregularities increased to GH¢18.4bn (approximately $1.66bn) in 2024 from GH¢8.8bn (approximately $790m) the previous year. The reported financial irregularities encompass a range of breaches of financial rules and procedures, meaning they do not necessarily indicate confirmed financial losses or misappropriation in every case. According to the report, the irregularities arose from breaches of financial management procedures, procurement shortcomings, contract management weaknesses and failures to comply with public financial management regulations. The Auditor-General also classified GH¢15.57bn (approximately $1.40bn) of the reported irregularities as recoverable, indicating that the office believes those amounts could potentially be reclaimed through corrective action or enforcement, subject to subsequent administrative or legal processes. Internal auditors are expected to identify many such weaknesses before they are detected in external audits, making effective internal controls a critical component of sound public-sector financial management. Wider governance reforms underway Alongside the proposed Auditors’ Court, the newly inaugurated IAA board has been mandated to strengthen institutional capacity and review the agency’s legal framework to improve compliance, risk management and value-for-money auditing across government entities. The initiative forms part of Ghana’s broader efforts to reinforce fiscal discipline and rebuild confidence in public financial administration. Those efforts have coincided with Ghana’s Fitch ratings upgrade amid fiscal reforms, which cited stronger public financial management and debt restructuring progress. The reforms also align with measures pursued under Ghana’s economic recovery programme and broader efforts to restore credibility after the country’s debt crisis. The accountability agenda complements Ghana’s drive to rebuild economic credibility after debt distress, which government officials argue is essential to sustaining investor confidence and long-term growth. During engagements with Ghanaian authorities in 2025, the IMF highlighted the importance of addressing structural weaknesses in public financial management as part of ongoing reform efforts. The government has already introduced additional fiscal safeguards, including amendments to the Bank of Ghana Act that tighten restrictions on central bank financing of government expenditure and strengthen oversight provisions. The reforms have unfolded alongside a wider debt restructuring programme. Africa Briefing previously reported on Ghana’s debt restructuring agreement with Belgium, one of several measures aimed at restoring fiscal sustainability and strengthening economic resilience. Whether the proposal is ultimately enacted remains uncertain, but it underscores the government’s broader effort to strengthen public financial oversight as part of ongoing fiscal and governance reforms.The post Ghana weighs Auditors’ Court after GH¢18.4bn in reported irregularities first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Dasa mine life has been extended from 12 to 23 years Revised study values the project at approximately $917m after tax Niger is positioning itself for a uranium sector revival amid growing global nuclear demand THE life of Niger’s Dasa uranium project has nearly doubled to 23 years after a revised feasibility study increased reserves and improved project economics, strengthening the outlook for one of Africa’s largest undeveloped uranium deposits. The update comes as Niger seeks to revive its uranium industry following the 2023 military takeover and growing tensions with French nuclear fuel company Orano. The project is also drawing attention from investors and utilities seeking new uranium supplies amid a global resurgence in nuclear energy. Dasa emerges as a strategic asset Located in the Agadez region, the Dasa uranium project has long been regarded as one of the highest-grade uranium deposits under development globally. According to Global Atomic’s June 2026 updated feasibility study, proven and probable reserves increased by approximately 50 percent to 73 million pounds of uranium oxide. Lifetime production increased by 55 percent to 68.1 million pounds, while the projected mine life expanded from 12 years to more than 23 years. The revised study also highlighted stronger project economics. Using a uranium price assumption of $75 per pound, Global Atomic estimated an after-tax net present value of approximately $917m and an internal rate of return of 57 percent, figures that place Dasa among the most attractive undeveloped uranium projects in the global market. Industry observers have long regarded Dasa as one of the highest-grade uranium projects under development globally, positioning it to benefit from improving market conditions and rising long-term demand. A sector seeking renewal Niger has historically ranked among the world’s leading uranium-producing nations, supplying fuel used in nuclear power stations across Europe and beyond. However, the country’s uranium industry has undergone major changes in recent years. Relations between French nuclear fuel company Orano and Niger’s military-led government have deteriorated significantly since the July 2023 coup. Disputes over mining concessions and resource control have become emblematic of a wider reassessment of Niger’s economic relationships with former colonial powers, including Niger’s revocation of a long-standing French uranium concession. The tensions reflect a broader trend across the Sahel, where governments have increasingly embraced resource nationalism and sought greater control over strategic mineral assets, reflecting the wider rise in resource nationalism risks across Africa. For Niger, the Dasa project represents an opportunity to demonstrate that major mining investment can continue despite political uncertainty and changing geopolitical alliances. Beyond France The Niger uranium project sits within a broader geopolitical realignment unfolding across West Africa. For decades, Niger was an important supplier of uranium to France’s nuclear industry. While France has diversified its supply chains over time, uranium remains a strategically sensitive commodity for countries seeking secure and reliable energy sources. Since the 2023 coup, Niger has pursued a foreign policy centred on greater sovereignty and diversified international partnerships, including new nuclear and uranium cooperation agreements with Russia. At the same time, countries including China, Russia, Turkey and several Gulf states have expanded their economic and diplomatic engagement across the Sahel. As competition for critical minerals intensifies globally, uranium has become increasingly important to governments seeking secure access to energy transition materials and nuclear fuel supplies. The Niger uranium project is therefore attracting attention not only from mining investors but also from governments concerned about long-term energy security and supply chain resilience, amid a broader trend of Africa tightening control over strategic mineral assets. Against this backdrop, Dasa is more than a mining project. It has become a test case for whether large-scale foreign investment can continue to flow into Niger under a changing political and economic order. Rising nuclear demand strengthens the case The project’s improving outlook coincides with renewed global enthusiasm for nuclear energy. Governments across Europe, North America and Asia are extending reactor lifespans, approving new facilities and investing in next-generation nuclear technologies. Growing electricity demand, decarbonisation targets and energy security concerns have all contributed to stronger uranium market fundamentals. Utilities are increasingly seeking long-term supply agreements, improving the economics of new uranium developments and enhancing the strategic importance of countries capable of bringing additional supply to market. For Niger, the timing could prove advantageous. Financing remains the final hurdle Despite the favourable feasibility study, important challenges remain before commercial production begins. Construction activity slowed following the 2023 coup and subsequent regional sanctions. Although many restrictions have since been lifted, securing the remaining financing required to complete development remains a critical milestone. Global Atomic has continued underground development work and site preparation while pursuing the funding needed to complete construction and advance the project towards production. The project is expected to generate significant export earnings for Niger and create hundreds of direct and indirect jobs once fully operational, adding to its importance within the country’s economic development strategy. Investors will therefore focus closely on financing progress over the next 12 to 24 months as the project moves towards its next phase. A pivotal moment for the Niger uranium project The revised feasibility study suggests that the Niger uranium project is closer to becoming a major new source of global uranium supply than at any point in recent years. For Niger’s government, successful development would provide export revenues, employment opportunities and evidence that international investors remain willing to commit capital to the country’s mining sector. For global uranium markets, Dasa could emerge as one of the most significant new projects entering production this decade. Whether the mine ultimately fulfils that promise will depend on financing, execution and political stability. Yet the latest study suggests Niger could play a larger role in global uranium supply just as governments worldwide are turning back to nuclear energy to strengthen energy security and meet climate goals.The post Niger extends uranium mine life to 23 years first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Africa’s mobile sector is projected to contribute $290bn by 2030 The continent’s biggest challenge has shifted from network coverage to digital adoption Mobile operators are expected to invest more than $76bn in infrastructure by 2030 AFRICA’S mobile sector is projected to contribute $290bn to the continent’s economy by 2030, up from $240bn in 2025, as operators shift their focus from expanding network coverage to increasing digital adoption, according to the GSMA’s latest Mobile Economy Africa findings. The sector contributed 7.8 percent of Africa’s GDP in 2025, underlining its growing importance to the continent’s economic future. Connectivity alone is no longer enough The findings highlight a major shift in Africa’s digital development. While mobile broadband networks now reach most of the population, the industry’s biggest challenge has become encouraging people to use available services. The GSMA estimates that 63 percent of Africans who live within mobile broadband coverage still do not use mobile internet services, compared with just 9 percent who remain outside coverage areas altogether. The report underscores how the continent’s digital future will depend not only on infrastructure investment but also on ensuring citizens have the tools, knowledge and resources needed to benefit from connectivity. Affordability constraints, limited digital skills and social barriers are increasingly preventing millions of Africans from participating in the digital economy despite living within network coverage areas. Similar concerns were highlighted in Inclusion is key to Africa’s digital future, which argues that meaningful connectivity requires affordability, digital literacy and locally relevant content. The GSMA said the mobile industry remains a critical driver of economic growth and digital inclusion across Africa, highlighting the sector’s expanding role in development, innovation and job creation. Usage gap replaces coverage challenge The figures suggest Africa’s digital divide is increasingly being defined by usage rather than availability. Industry analysts note that factors such as the cost of smartphones, data affordability, digital literacy and access to locally relevant content continue to influence adoption rates across many African markets. Bringing more Africans online could unlock billions of dollars in additional economic activity while expanding access to education, healthcare, financial services and government platforms. Mobile money continues to be one of the most significant drivers of digital adoption across Africa, particularly in East and West Africa, where digital financial services have helped millions gain access to formal financial systems for the first time. The rapid expansion of digital payments is also reshaping commerce, as highlighted in Africa wallets power prepaid payments surge, which examines how mobile wallets are becoming gateways to the broader digital economy. Mobile sector’s economic footprint grows The mobile ecosystem remains a significant economic driver across the continent. According to the GSMA, the sector contributed $240bn to Africa’s economy in 2025, equivalent to 7.8 percent of GDP. It also supported approximately 13 million jobs and generated $45bn in public revenues through taxes, fees and spectrum-related payments. The figures highlight the growing role of telecommunications infrastructure in supporting economic diversification and productivity growth. Countries including Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa and Egypt have emerged as some of Africa’s leading digital economy hubs, supported by growing smartphone adoption, mobile money services, fintech innovation and expanding broadband access. Broader forecasts suggest the continent’s digital economy could expand dramatically over the next decade, as explored in Africa’s digital economy to hit $1.5 trillion. Mobile connectivity now underpins a wide range of industries, including financial technology, agriculture, e-commerce, logistics and digital health services. Operators evolve into digital partners The findings indicate that mobile operators are increasingly repositioning themselves as broader digital transformation partners rather than simply providers of voice and data services. More than three-quarters of operators surveyed identified digital transformation as a core strategic objective. Many are investing in artificial intelligence, cloud-based services, fintech platforms and open-network models designed to support innovation and enterprise growth. Similar trends are evident in the financial sector, where partnerships such as Ecobank’s collaboration with Google Cloud are accelerating digital transformation across multiple African markets. The shift reflects changing consumer behaviour and growing demand for integrated digital services across Africa’s rapidly expanding digital economy. Strategic competition intensifies The forecast comes as African governments increasingly view digital infrastructure as a strategic asset amid growing competition among global technology companies, cloud providers, mobile operators and satellite internet firms seeking a larger presence across the continent. The contest for Africa’s digital future is attracting investment from international technology giants, regional telecom groups and emerging satellite broadband providers, all seeking to expand services in one of the world’s fastest-growing digital markets. Countries are also accelerating efforts to develop digital economy strategies aimed at boosting innovation, improving public services and attracting technology investment. The race to expand digital capabilities is becoming an important component of broader economic competitiveness, with governments seeking to ensure that local businesses and citizens benefit from technological transformation. Investment momentum remains strong Despite progress in network expansion, investment remains central to the sector’s future growth. The GSMA estimates that operators across Africa will invest more than $76bn in network infrastructure by 2030. Much of the spending is expected to support the continued expansion of 4G services, targeted deployment of 5G networks and improvements in network quality and capacity. Industry leaders argue that sustained investment will be necessary to support rising demand for data services and emerging technologies. However, the report suggests that infrastructure spending alone will not be sufficient to close Africa’s digital divide. Instead, the next phase of growth will depend on making connectivity more affordable, improving digital skills and creating services that address the everyday needs of African consumers and businesses. If those barriers can be overcome, the GSMA believes the mobile sector will continue to serve as one of Africa’s most important engines of economic growth, innovation and job creation through the end of the decade. Analysts expect demand for mobile internet, digital payments, cloud services and AI-powered applications to accelerate across Africa during the remainder of the decade, creating new opportunities for businesses, governments and consumers. Whether the continent reaches the projected $290bn contribution will depend largely on how successfully operators, policymakers and technology providers can convert network access into meaningful digital participation and economic activity.The post Africa’s mobile economy to reach $290bn first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: African ministers adopt a new roadmap to lower air travel costs IATA warns political barriers continue to undermine reforms SAATM implementation remains crucial to unlocking growth AFRICAN ministers ended the African Air Transport Convention and Expo 2026 by adopting a roadmap to lower air travel costs and improve connectivity, renewing efforts to create a single aviation market across the continent. The Lomé Ministerial Declaration and Implementation Matrix seek to accelerate the Single African Air Transport Market (SAATM), but industry leaders say political resistance, high taxes and slow implementation continue to undermine efforts to create a more competitive and affordable aviation sector. A renewed push for African aviation integration The declaration was adopted on June 16 at the close of the African Air Transport Convention and Expo 2026 in Lomé, where ministers responsible for transport, tourism, trade and finance from African Union member states gathered to discuss the future of African aviation. The agreement seeks to accelerate implementation of the Single African Air Transport Market (SAATM), a flagship African Union initiative designed to liberalise air services and improve connectivity across Africa. Ministers reaffirmed their commitment to the full implementation of the Yamoussoukro Decision and SAATM, while pledging to remove restrictive market access barriers, liberalise air services and improve administrative processes governing airline operations. They also committed to improving visa openness, passenger facilitation, cargo clearance systems and digital travel platforms to support continental integration. The agreement reflects growing recognition that aviation is not simply a transport issue but a strategic enabler of trade, tourism, investment and economic integration under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). Ministers also described aviation as a critical driver of industrialisation and regional value chains, linking air connectivity to broader economic transformation goals. Yet despite repeated commitments over the past two decades, implementation has often fallen short. Africa Briefing previously reported that visa restrictions, protectionism and uneven implementation continue to hinder aviation liberalisation despite broad support for SAATM across the continent. Passenger demand is not the problem The timing of the declaration coincides with strong growth prospects for African aviation. According to projections highlighted by the International Air Transport Association (IATA), passenger traffic across Africa is expected to grow by 6.0 percent in 2026, outpacing the projected global average of 4.9 percent. The figures suggest demand for air travel remains robust despite economic headwinds in many markets. Yet profitability tells a different story. African airlines are expected to generate only about $200 million of the estimated $41 bn in global airline profits this year, equivalent to a regional profit margin of around 1.0 percent. By comparison, airlines worldwide are expected to earn an average of $7.90 per passenger, while African carriers are projected to earn only about $1.30. The disparity highlights a central challenge confronting policymakers: demand is growing, but the commercial environment remains difficult. Africa is home to roughly 18 percent of the world’s population but accounts for only a small share of global air traffic, underlining the scale of the continent’s connectivity gap. Politics remains aviation’s biggest challenge In an interview with Ecofin Agency, Kamil Al-Awadhi, IATA’s Regional Vice President for Africa and the Middle East, argued that political barriers continue to constrain African aviation despite widespread recognition of the sector’s economic importance. One of the principal concerns remains uneven implementation of SAATM. Although many governments have signed agreements supporting aviation liberalisation, some continue to protect national carriers through regulatory restrictions that limit competition and market access. ‘The challenge is not signing agreements. The challenge is implementing them,’ Al-Awadhi told Ecofin Agency. The result is a fragmented aviation landscape where many African cities remain poorly connected and passengers are frequently forced to transit through hubs outside the continent to reach neighbouring countries. This fragmentation increases costs, reduces route viability and limits the economic benefits aviation can deliver. The Lomé Declaration directly acknowledges these concerns by committing governments to remove restrictive barriers and align air service agreements with SAATM principles. High charges continue to keep fares elevated Another area where the declaration and industry concerns overlap is the cost of air travel. Ministers recognised that high aviation taxes, fees and charges, together with operational bottlenecks, increase the cost of both passenger travel and air freight while suppressing demand. To address the issue, governments endorsed a Continental Harmonised Policy Framework on Aviation Taxes, Charges and Fees designed to promote more transparent and growth-oriented approaches to aviation charges. Al-Awadhi has similarly argued that excessive taxation remains a major obstacle to sector growth. ‘ECOWAS has already taken the decision. The issue is implementation,’ he said, referring to agreed reductions in aviation-related charges across the regional bloc. The consequence is that many intra-African routes remain relatively expensive despite comparatively short distances. Visa reforms could unlock new growth The declaration also places significant emphasis on improving mobility across Africa. Ministers committed to advancing visa openness, passenger facilitation and more efficient border management systems. Industry leaders view such reforms as potentially transformative. ‘If Africans can travel freely across Africa, traffic will grow,’ Al-Awadhi said, arguing that liberalised visa policies could increase intra-African passenger traffic by between 6 and 8 percent. Easier travel procedures would complement AfCFTA by helping entrepreneurs, investors and professionals move more efficiently across borders. For many analysts, liberalising mobility may prove just as important as liberalising air services themselves. Cargo corridors and AfCFTA ambitions Beyond passenger travel, the Lomé roadmap places considerable emphasis on air cargo development. Ministers committed to supporting priority intra-African cargo corridors aligned with AfCFTA value chains and regional economic priorities. The declaration encourages stronger collaboration among airlines, airports, cargo operators, regulators and financial institutions to strengthen route development and logistics infrastructure. Improved cargo connectivity could play a vital role in supporting manufacturing, agriculture, pharmaceuticals and e-commerce sectors seeking access to regional markets. Recent gains in intra-African connectivity are already helping position cities such as Nairobi as emerging hubs for trade, tourism and regional mobility. Airlines such as Ethiopian Airlines, ASKY Airlines, Kenya Airways and Air Côte d’Ivoire could benefit from greater market access if governments fully implement SAATM commitments. Sustainable aviation fuel presents an opportunity The declaration also highlights Africa’s growing interest in sustainable aviation. Governments committed to supporting the development, financing and deployment of Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) and other lower-carbon aviation energy solutions. Industry observers believe Africa’s agricultural resources could position the continent as a future SAF producer. If developed successfully, domestic SAF production could improve energy security, reduce fuel import dependence and create new industrial opportunities. However, achieving those ambitions will require significant investment, regulatory certainty and internationally recognised certification systems. Funding and accountability will be crucial One of the declaration’s most important outcomes was the launch of the AFCAC Solidarity Commitment 2026-2028, a resource mobilisation initiative intended to strengthen AFCAC’s capacity to support member states, accelerate SAATM implementation and advance continental aviation priorities. The initiative seeks to mobilise financial resources, technical assistance, capacity-building support, systems and project financing in a transparent and results-oriented manner. Continental efforts to reduce airline operating costs are also gathering momentum through broader airspace modernisation initiatives designed to improve efficiency and strengthen regional integration. AFCAC has also been tasked with coordinating implementation efforts and preparing a post-Lomé roadmap identifying priority actions, timelines, responsible institutions and reporting mechanisms. That emphasis on financing and measurable implementation may ultimately determine whether the initiative succeeds where previous reforms struggled. As Al-Awadhi’s assessment suggests, Africa’s aviation challenge is no longer a lack of passengers. Passenger demand continues to grow, but policy and regulatory barriers continue to limit the sector’s potential. The question now is whether governments will finally match their commitments with sustained reforms that open markets, reduce costs and remove barriers to movement. If they can, the Lomé Declaration could become a turning point for African aviation. If they cannot, the continent risks continuing to generate strong traffic growth while capturing only a fraction of the sector’s economic potential.The post African ministers push cheaper flights across Africa first appeared on Africa Briefing.
